questionText: What does inheritance allow in OOP?
option1: A class to acquire properties and behaviors of another class
option2: A class to run multiple threads
option3: A class to encrypt its data
option4: A class to remove properties from another class
correctOptionExplanation: Inheritance lets a subclass acquire (reuse) the fields and methods of a superclass.

questionText: Which keyword is used to implement inheritance between two classes in Java?
option4: implements
correctOptionExplanation: The extends keyword is used for class inheritance in Java.

questionText: What relationship does inheritance model?
option4: USES-A
correctOptionExplanation: Inheritance models an IS-A relationship, e.g., a Car IS-A Vehicle.

questionText: How many classes can a single Java class directly extend?
option4: Only one
correctOptionExplanation: Java supports single inheritance for classes; a class can extend only one direct superclass.

questionText: How does Java achieve multiple inheritance of type?
option4: Through multiple extends
correctOptionExplanation: Java allows a class to implement multiple interfaces, achieving multiple inheritance of type (not implementation).

questionText: What is the primary use of the super keyword?
option4: To refer to the immediate parent class
correctOptionExplanation: super refers to the immediate parent class and is used to access its members or constructor.

questionText: What does super() do when called inside a subclass constructor?
option4: Declares a static block
correctOptionExplanation: super() invokes the constructor of the immediate superclass.

questionText: If a subclass constructor doesn't explicitly call super() or this(), what happens?
option1: The object is created without calling any constructor
option2: The compiler inserts an implicit no-arg super() call
option4: The JVM throws a runtime exception
correctOptionExplanation: The compiler automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor if none is specified.

questionText: In which order are constructors executed in an inheritance chain?
option4: Order is undefined
correctOptionExplanation: The parent class constructor always completes before the child class constructor body executes.

questionText: Can constructors be inherited by a subclass?
option4: Yes, always
correctOptionExplanation: Constructors are never inherited; each class defines its own, though it may call the parent's via super().

questionText: What is method overriding?
option3: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameters
option4: Redefining a parent class method in the subclass with the same signature
correctOptionExplanation: Overriding means a subclass provides a specific implementation for a method already defined in its superclass, with the same signature.

questionText: What is the key difference between overriding and overloading?
option1: Overriding involves the same signature across parent/child; overloading involves different parameter lists within the same class
option3: Overriding changes return type only; overloading changes method name
option4: Overloading only works with inheritance; overriding does not
correctOptionExplanation: Overriding is runtime polymorphism between super/subclass with identical signatures; overloading is compile-time polymorphism within the same class using different parameter lists.

questionText: What does the @Override annotation do?
option1: Forces the method to become private
option3: Prevents the subclass from being instantiated
option4: Tells the compiler to verify the method actually overrides a superclass method
correctOptionExplanation: @Override is a compile-time check ensuring the annotated method correctly overrides a superclass method, catching typos or signature mismatches.

questionText: When overriding a method, can the subclass reduce its access modifier (e.g., public to private)?
option1: Yes, but only for static methods
option4: No, the access level can only stay the same or become more permissive
correctOptionExplanation: Java disallows narrowing visibility during overriding to preserve the superclass's contract (Liskov substitution).

questionText: What happens if you mark a method as final in a superclass?
option1: It cannot be overridden by any subclass
option3: It can only be called once
option4: It is automatically inherited as private
correctOptionExplanation: A final method cannot be overridden in any subclass.

questionText: What happens if you mark a class as final?
option2: The class cannot have any methods
option4: The class cannot be instantiated
correctOptionExplanation: A final class cannot be subclassed at all.

questionText: Are private members of a superclass inherited (accessible) by a subclass?
option1: No, they are deleted from the object
option3: They exist in the object but are not directly accessible by name in the subclass
option4: Only if the subclass is in the same file
correctOptionExplanation: Private members are part of the object's memory layout but can't be accessed directly by the subclass, only via public/protected getters or methods.

questionText: What is method hiding in the context of static methods?
option1: When a method is made private in the subclass
option2: When a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a static method in the superclass, it hides rather than overrides it
option3: When a static method is deleted at runtime
option4: When an abstract method is hidden from documentation
correctOptionExplanation: Static methods are resolved at compile time based on reference type, so redefining them in a subclass hides (not overrides) the parent's version.

questionText: Which of the following can be truly overridden in Java?
option4: Private methods
correctOptionExplanation: Only instance (non-static, non-final, non-private) methods can be truly overridden; static methods are hidden, private methods aren't inherited, final methods can't be overridden.

questionText: What is the root class of every class hierarchy in Java?
option4: Class
correctOptionExplanation: Every class in Java implicitly extends java.lang.Object if no other superclass is specified.

questionText: What does the instanceof operator check?
option4: Whether an object is an instance of a specific class or subclass
correctOptionExplanation: instanceof tests if an object is an instance of a given class, subclass, or implementing class of an interface.

questionText: What is upcasting in inheritance?
option1: Assigning a subclass object reference to a superclass type variable
option2: Converting a String to an int
option3: Casting a static method to an instance method
option4: Assigning a superclass object to a subclass variable directly
correctOptionExplanation: Upcasting refers to treating a subclass instance as its superclass type, e.g., Animal a = new Dog(); which is always safe.

questionText: What is downcasting?
option2: Casting a superclass reference back to a subclass type, which may require an explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException
option4: Casting a subclass to superclass implicitly
correctOptionExplanation: Downcasting converts a superclass reference to a subclass type explicitly, and is unsafe unless the actual object really is of that subclass.

questionText: Can an abstract class be instantiated directly?
option2: Yes, but only with a static factory
option4: Yes, always
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated; they exist to be extended by concrete subclasses.

questionText: If a subclass extends an abstract class, what must it do with the abstract methods?
option2: Implement all abstract methods, or itself be declared abstract
option4: Convert them to static methods
correctOptionExplanation: A concrete subclass must implement every abstract method it inherits; otherwise it must also be declared abstract.

questionText: What's a key difference between an abstract class and a traditional interface (pre-Java 8 default methods)?
option1: Abstract classes can be instantiated directly
option3: An abstract class can have constructors and instance state; a traditional interface cannot
option4: Interfaces support multiple inheritance of state; abstract classes do not
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes can hold constructors, instance fields, and partial implementations, while traditional interfaces only declared method signatures with no state.

questionText: What is the diamond problem?
option1: Ambiguity that arises when a class inherits the same method from two different parent paths
option2: An error thrown when a class has too many fields
option3: A performance issue in deeply nested loops
option4: A naming convention for interfaces
correctOptionExplanation: The diamond problem occurs in multiple inheritance when a class inherits conflicting implementations of the same method from two ancestors, creating ambiguity about which to use.

questionText: How does Java avoid the classic diamond problem for classes?
option1: By allowing multiple class inheritance freely
option4: By deprecating the extends keyword
correctOptionExplanation: Java sidesteps the diamond problem by only permitting single inheritance of classes; interfaces with default methods require the implementing class to explicitly resolve conflicts.

questionText: A protected member of a superclass is accessible to:
option2: Subclasses (even in different packages) and classes in the same package
option4: No one outside the file
correctOptionExplanation: protected grants access to subclasses regardless of package, plus any class within the same package.

questionText: Why is favor composition over inheritance a common design guideline?
option1: Inheritance cannot be used in Java
option2: Composition creates looser coupling and avoids fragile base class problems
option3: Composition is always faster at runtime
option4: Composition eliminates the need for interfaces
correctOptionExplanation: Composition (HAS-A) tends to be more flexible and less brittle than deep inheritance hierarchies, which can break when a base class changes.

questionText: What is hierarchical inheritance?
option1: One superclass has multiple subclasses inheriting from it
option3: A subclass inherits from multiple superclasses
option4: A chain of classes each inheriting from the previous
correctOptionExplanation: Hierarchical inheritance is when one parent class is extended by several distinct child classes.

questionText: What is multilevel inheritance?
option1: Two classes inheriting from the same parent
option2: A chain where a class inherits from a subclass, which itself inherits from another class
option4: A static inheritance pattern
correctOptionExplanation: Multilevel inheritance forms a chain: e.g., Class C extends Class B, and Class B extends Class A.

questionText: Can a class in Java extend itself (e.g., class A extends A)?
option1: Yes, but only for abstract classes
option2: Yes, it's a valid recursive class
option3: No, this causes a compile-time error
option4: Only allowed with generics
correctOptionExplanation: A class cannot extend itself; Java detects this cyclic inheritance and raises a compile-time error.

questionText: How does inheritance enable runtime polymorphism?
option1: Polymorphism only works with static methods
option2: A superclass reference can point to different subclass objects, and the overridden method actually invoked is determined at runtime
option3: Inheritance has nothing to do with polymorphism
option4: It requires the final keyword
correctOptionExplanation: Because subclasses override superclass methods, a superclass-typed reference calling that method invokes the actual subclass's version at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

questionText: Are instance fields polymorphic like overridden methods (resolved by actual object type)?
option1: No, field access is resolved based on the reference type, not the actual object type
option3: Yes, fields behave exactly like overridden methods
option4: Only final fields are polymorphic
correctOptionExplanation: Unlike methods, fields are not polymorphic; accessing a field through a superclass reference always gets the superclass's field, even if a subclass hides it with a same-named field.

questionText: What does this() do inside a constructor (as opposed to super())?
option2: Calls another constructor in the same class
option4: Calls the parent class constructor
correctOptionExplanation: this() is used for constructor chaining within the same class, while super() calls the parent class's constructor.

questionText: Can a constructor call be both this() and super() in the same constructor?
option1: Yes, but only in abstract classes
option3: Yes, both can appear together anywhere
option4: No, only one of them can be used per constructor, and it must be the first statement
correctOptionExplanation: A constructor may call either this() or super(), but only one, and it must be the very first statement.

questionText: Can a subclass override a constructor from its superclass?
option4: No, constructors are not inherited or overridden
correctOptionExplanation: Constructors aren't inherited, so the concept of overriding doesn't apply to them; each class must define its own constructors.

questionText: In Java 8+, what feature allows interfaces to provide method bodies (partial implementation of behavior)?
option4: Abstract methods
correctOptionExplanation: Java 8 introduced default methods in interfaces, letting interfaces provide a method body that implementing classes can use or override.

questionText: Can interfaces have static methods?
option2: Only if the interface is marked final
option3: No, interfaces can never have static methods
option4: Yes, since Java 8
correctOptionExplanation: Since Java 8, interfaces can declare static methods, callable directly on the interface itself.

questionText: Can a single class implement multiple interfaces in Java?
option2: No, only one interface per class
option4: Only if the interfaces have no methods
correctOptionExplanation: A class can implement any number of interfaces, which is how Java achieves multiple inheritance of type.

questionText: What are covariant return types in method overriding?
option1: An overriding method may return a subtype of the return type declared in the superclass method
option3: The overriding method must always throw the same exceptions
option4: Return types must exactly match with no variation allowed
correctOptionExplanation: Since Java 5, an overriding method can return a more specific (subclass) type than the overridden method's declared return type; this is called a covariant return type.

questionText: When overriding a method that declares checked exceptions, what rule applies to the subclass method?
option1: It cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions than the superclass method
option2: Checked exceptions are ignored during overriding
option3: It must throw at least one checked exception
option4: It can throw any exception type freely
correctOptionExplanation: An overriding method cannot declare new or broader checked exceptions than the method it overrides, to preserve substitutability.

questionText: If a subclass defines a private method with the same name and parameters as a private method in its superclass, what happens?
option2: It becomes a static method automatically
option3: It overrides the parent's private method
option4: It's a completely independent method, not an override, since private methods aren't inherited
correctOptionExplanation: Since private methods aren't visible to or inherited by the subclass, defining a same-named private method in the subclass is unrelated to the parent's; no overriding occurs.

questionText: What is the purpose of super.methodName() inside an overriding method?
option3: To call a static method only
option4: To explicitly call the superclass's version of the overridden method
correctOptionExplanation: super.methodName() lets an overriding method still invoke and build upon the parent class's original implementation.

questionText: How does inheritance interact with encapsulation?
option2: Encapsulation is only possible without inheritance
option4: Inheritance can weaken encapsulation if superclass internals are overexposed via protected or public members
correctOptionExplanation: Careless use of protected/public fields in a superclass can leak implementation details to subclasses, weakening encapsulation, a known criticism of deep inheritance hierarchies.

questionText: Which is a classic real-world example of inheritance?
option4: Car extends Vehicle
correctOptionExplanation: Car extends Vehicle is a textbook IS-A example; a Car is a specialized kind of Vehicle.

questionText: What is the main risk of overusing deep inheritance hierarchies?
option4: Tight coupling and fragile base class problems, where superclass changes break many subclasses
correctOptionExplanation: Deep inheritance chains tightly couple subclasses to superclass implementation details, so changes to the base class can unexpectedly break many descendants (fragile base class problem).

questionText: When should you generally prefer inheritance over composition?
option1: Always, inheritance is preferred in every case
option2: Never, inheritance should always be avoided
option3: When there's a true IS-A relationship and the subclass needs to reuse and extend base behavior polymorphically
option4: Whenever two classes share any field name
correctOptionExplanation: Inheritance fits best for genuine IS-A relationships where polymorphic substitution is needed; otherwise composition (HAS-A) is usually more flexible.

questionText: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle state in relation to inheritance?
option1: Subclasses must always override every method
option2: Interfaces must not have default methods
option4: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking the program's correctness
correctOptionExplanation: LSP states that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program, a core principle guiding proper inheritance design.
